drug_class: Immune checkpoint inhibitor (PD-L1 blocker) / Immunotherapy / Monoclonal antibody
purpose: Durvalumab is a cancer-fighting medicine used to treat certain types of lung cancer, liver cancer, biliary tract cancer, and small cell lung cancer. It is given when the cancer cannot be removed with surgery or has spread. It is often used alone or combined with chemotherapy to help slow or stop cancer growth.
how_it_works: Your immune system has natural 'brakes' that cancer cells can hijack to hide from it. Durvalumab works by blocking one of those brakes called PD-L1, which releases your immune system so it can recognize and attack cancer cells more effectively. Think of it like taking the handcuffs off your immune system so it can do its job fighting the cancer.
common_side_effects: Feeling tired or weak, cough, shortness of breath, nausea, diarrhea, constipation, decreased appetite, rash or itchy skin, urinary tract infections, swelling in arms or legs, and abnormal liver or thyroid blood test results.
warnings: Because this medicine supercharges your immune system, it can sometimes cause your immune system to attack healthy organs — this is called an immune reaction. This can affect your lungs, liver, intestines, kidneys, thyroid, or other organs and can be serious or life-threatening. Tell your doctor right away if you have new or worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, severe diarrhea, yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, or any unusual symptoms. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby.
typical_dosing: Durvalumab is given through an IV (intravenous infusion) at a clinic or hospital — not taken as a pill at home. The dose depends on your weight and the type of cancer being treated. A common schedule is once every 2 to 4 weeks, with each infusion taking about 1 hour. Your cancer care team will determine the exact dose and schedule right for you.
